author: buchanan_robert
text:
Then I came back from wandering through the woods,

Where the wild lilies grow, where the wild orchids bloom,
To a great house in which I had been living long;

But the door stood open wide to let the summer wind
Blow through, and I felt that I had lost my way,

author: cushag
text:
The great red sun rose flaming above the water,

Blazed on the face of every cliff and crag,

Blew fiercely through the forest, struck the meadow,

Lashed all the river with its glare and warmth,—

Then passed away! It was so hot, I thought,

That no man could live who did not wear a hat!

But soon after came a storm which blew with fury

From the sea, as if it were determined,

If it could not have what it asked for, to blast

Everything that lived or had lived in Ireland.

He will not come back again, nor ever more.

His life is all done up, and finished for ever,

But there is nothing I can do or say here—

For that child may come back, for this much is certain,

That as long as the great sun burns on in heaven,

The little ones who have grown old, though they perish,

Will never be forgotten! But we shall see them,

In our dreams of night, still beautiful as children,

Still young and happy, when we lost them for ever.

author: buchanan_robert
text:
THE WICKED WIFE AND HER CHILDREN.

There is none but I know how the wicked wife

Has used us all, so that our tears are dry.

To you, O! Lord, this tale we will unfold.

How, when my father died, my dear old mother

Came home at night and wept before her children

For the death of him who gave them bread and meat;

She said, “My little ones, God hath taken one

Of your dear parents—but He still preserves

The other for your use, and mine!” And then

author: cushag
text:
" Me husband an' mi was marrited
Mony a year agone ;

We had ma-ny a fine lummper o' clildren,
But they are now all gone.

Oh! whan I look on me poor husband's face,
I feel like to die;

For he's so tall and thin that his head looks as big
As a two-year-old filly."

author: cushag
text:
Old Mother Brown an' her daughters three
Sat down to sew one winter's night ;

While in came Nan with wet hair an' red eyes,

Sayin', "I love you all, but I can't abide."

"What did ye do wi' poor Tom?" said old Mrs. Brown;

"The devil took him!" cried Nan, "an' it's my own !"

Her mother looked round on Mary and Grace,

But they were all quiet as any mice!

author: emily_dickinson
text:
The old woman took her bundle down;
She had lived many a long year,
And made herself content with what she found--
 She knew no other way than this to steer!

 In every tree that’s green;

text:
This is my garden! God made it, -
 It lies before my door;
 A little patch of ground, where grows
 The white anemone poor.
 To others this would be no place
 For such as me to stay,
 But for me it's a home, a place
 Where dreams can live away.

author: emily_dickinson
text:

 A little cloudlet white,

 Though it might be your own,

author: john_masefield
text:
While yet I was in thought alone, my door
Opened: I sprung up, but it was only Tom,
My page; who brought me tidings from the Queen:

author: john_keats
text: I have been at length so good as to make you an offer of ten guineas, for which I beg leave to ask your answer in a letter directed from Bath, where I am, to Mr. William Godwin, Red Lion Court, Fleet Street; but not before it is sealed and delivered, do not trust yourself upon any promise that may be made to you after this date. Do me the favour to send my answer immediately, or it will be too late.

author: john_keats
text:
The courtier’s eyes, at first astonished, flash;
Then they are calm, but not from any bashfulness,
For he knows well their lord is nothing mean,
But just as great a lord as ever Queen Joan met.

author: john_masefield
text:
"At eleven o'clock my brother died
As the last sun was setting, dying;
His head dropped back upon his pillow,
He said that he felt better.

The clock in the window struck six,
My brother lay upon the bed,
The doctor came, and he looked at him,
And said, "He is dead."

I get a big bowl of soup,
There are fresh potatoes in it,
But no carrots or cabbage;
I have milk for my supper,
With bread and butter,
We never go hungry,
Because she's dead poor.'

author: john_masefield

text:
This is what I have been doing all my life.
It’s a matter of pride with us, too; we are
the sons of seamen. It’s in our blood. We
don’t care who knows it or not.

I would rather see a ship sink than stay in
her as long as I was aboard her when she went
down, unless I had orders from someone above
me.”

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I was born in England, bred in the navy;

My father and mother were both sailors. . ..

I have lived upon the ocean, all my life,
With the waves beating at my feet,

Like my mother rocking me in her lap;
When the world was young, and free, and sweet,

I was born on board a merchantman,
Of which my father was the skipper;

The captain always calls his ship his own,
You may call it yours, and I will drop — oop!

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I wish to thank you very much for my
appointment as cook aboard your ship.

Please excuse me if I am too blunt with you,
but in my 40 years on land, I have seen
much worse than yourself. In fact, there is not

a soul alive who has treated his staff as badly
as you do! As it happens, this will be my last
voyage and I would love nothing better than to

die peacefully at sea. So, if you are so kind,

Could you please arrange my funeral in
accordance with my wishes?

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I will not leave this island before my time;
I have been here a hundred and one times

(To go on voyages, or just to look around)
When all the seas were young and brave and clean.

text: *In Homer's Odyssey we are told that Ulysses had "a great belly full of meat," and it is also said that "he did not touch food for nine days;" but in this passage from Lycophron no allusion can be made to either of these statements. The poet may have wished only to say that Philip's appetite was so good that he could eat what little he ate without much hunger or thirst; or else he may mean that, though his body had been treated harshly, it retained its vigour, as the muscles of men who work hard retain their strength and elasticity.

"The old man's gone now for good; and here she stands! -
With all her brothers and her sisters—so much joy!
It would break your heart if you only saw their faces,
As they stand about in this field so lonely!
Her father is away somewhere on his business,
And he'll be back again before many days.
She looks like an angel, but there are tears in her eyes.
How does she know? What does she think?"

author: robert_frost
text:
"But now they come from distant places—
The children in rags, and men who speak
Of all their sins as if they were not crimes;
They ask for bread. We know not where to send them.
We pity them, but we do not give them anything."

author: stephen_crane
text:
The king is dead long live the king!
 There was an echo from far off;
 An old woman went out on her way,
 And all the world was glad.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
A young girl was seated at her work table.

"Oh," she sighed, "I wish I could be rich and spend my days as we do on our farm. If you know what I mean?"

The voice of the Lord came clear and strong:

"Go out upon your porch and see for yourself!"

"One thing I cannot forget," cried an old woman,
And she began to speak and weep.
She told me about her husband who died when she was young;
But still she loved him, you see.

One day at dinner-time, as they sat there together,
Her son came into the room.
His face was white with terror, for he'd found his father dead
In a most strange and ghastly tomb.

When all had finished eating they went out to walk along,
As we often do, upon this ground.
The sun beat

author: stephen_crane
text:
Two old men, with wrinkled foreheads,
 On a stone sat down to rest;
 Each had his pipe and matchbook on hand,
 And stared into a distance so vast.
 It seemed as though they saw it all.

author: stephen_crane
text:
The night was dark as pitch,
 And the rain fell in torrents;
 The lightning flamed and flashed,
 The thunder rolled and roared,
 But the wind from out his bosom
 Fanned her cheek with every gust,
 Till she felt the zephyr kiss
 Her soft rosy lip for lust.

author: stothert_james_a
text:
"There are three great divisions of man's being ; body, mind and spirit ;
and there are two ways which we may adopt for training ourselves—the way of sense and the way of intellect. We can develop either or both. The intellectual faculty may be developed by itself, but this cannot satisfy the deepest cravings of human nature. There must be an awakening of the soul; then only will the intellect become a true instrument of good."

author: thomas_hardy
text: The Moon and I — we are together yet.

To God and Nature my song I raise ;

Love's music sounds through all the spheres ;
God's mighty laws of peace we praise,

His truth we hear in every verse.
But when from earth's dull circle we escape,

To realms above where angels dwell,
Then will the raptures of his face

Outshine the brightness of a star;
More lovely are his words than sun or moon,

Or lightnings which his power declare,
Which, though they pierce and melt like beams of noon,

Are not so sweet as when he speaks

 To gather shells and stones,—
 You might have heard me say:
 “I am not what you think I am!
 What shall be done if all is done?”

The heart that never had its bliss
 In any human face or form;
 The mind that could not find an eye
 To which it could impart its balm!

“Whence have I come?” “Why am I thus?” “What is this world?” In vain
I ask my soul! No answer comes. Then shall it be that none can know?

thomas_hardy
text:
They came who had not crossed
 The boundary that lies
 Between the world of flesh
 And soul beyond the skies;
 They came with hopes and fears
 That left their footsteps bare.

author: william_wordsworth
text: The Sea, O Sea! thou mighty Mother, Art thou a friend or foe? Is this thy power Which sweeps me o’er thy breast, when I am sore And panting in thy fury? Or art thou A soft embrace which soothes me like a dove When sorrow wakes me early from repose, With sighs for him whom thou hast taken from me ?

author: buchanan_robert
text:

 Oh, come, sweet star! from yonder burning zone,
 Come down into our land! for thou art known,
 Even now thou hearest us! we know thee well,
 We watch thee every day at evening fall;

 Yet didst thou wait till the last moment came.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
I met you in the morning
As you were coming from your room;
And while we talked together,
The words flew round about like leaves that fall
In autumn's tempest, or in summer's gale
When fruit-laden trees are shorn away.
For all your sorrow was around you then.
My heart grew heavy with distress and pain,
But though so much you had to bear,
Your eyes were bright, and your hair lay loose
Upon your shoulders. But when I looked at you,
Like those poor flowers which bloom only once,

author: william_wordsworth
text:
O! thou whose hand hath laid our country waste,
 Whose heart could turn so dark a scene to view,
 When all around was light--thou, unprovok’d,
 And unrepented, hast destroy’d our state;
 But not for ever. The Lord will give us grace,
 Nor shall his wrath abideth long in store.
